title: Measures of Central Tendency
description: Class 11 Economics: arithmetic mean and weighted mean, median and mode with worked examples, their merits and demerits, and how to compare mean, median and mode.

topics.title: Arithmetic Mean and Weighted Mean
topics.concept:
A mass of data is hard to grasp, so we summarise it with a single value that represents the whole — a measure of central tendency (an average). It is the central or typical value around which the data cluster. The three main averages are the mean, the median and the mode.

The arithmetic mean is the most common average. It is found by adding all the values and dividing by the number of values:

Mean (X̄) = ΣX ÷ N

where ΣX is the sum of all the values and N is the number of values. For example, the mean of 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 is (10 + 20 + 30 + 40 + 50) ÷ 5 = 150 ÷ 5 = 30.

Sometimes the items are not equally important. Then we use the weighted mean, where each value X is multiplied by its weight W (its importance):

Weighted Mean = ΣWX ÷ ΣW

For instance, if a student scores 80 in a 3-credit subject and 60 in a 1-credit subject, the simple mean (70) misjudges the result. The weighted mean = [(80×3) + (60×1)] ÷ (3 + 1) = (240 + 60) ÷ 4 = 300 ÷ 4 = 75, which gives the more important subject its proper weight. The mean is easy to calculate and uses every value, but its big weakness is that it is badly affected by extreme values (one very large or very small figure can distort it).

examples.solution:
Add the values and divide by how many there are.

  • ΣX = 5 + 15 + 25 + 35 = 80; N = 4.
  • Mean = 80 ÷ 4 = 20.

examples.problem: Example 2: Why is the arithmetic mean affected by extreme values? Illustrate.
examples.solution:
Every value enters the sum.

  • Data 10, 20, 30 has mean 20.
  • If 30 is replaced by 300, mean = (10+20+300)÷3 = 110 — one extreme value pulls the mean far up.
examples.answer: Because every value is added in, one extreme value (e.g. 300 instead of 30) can pull the mean far away from the typical value.

examples.problem: Example 3: A student scores 90 (weight 2) and 60 (weight 1). Find the weighted mean.

recap:
• Central tendency = a single value representing the whole data (mean, median, mode).
  • Arithmetic mean = ΣX ÷ N; uses every value, easy, but affected by extreme values.
  • Weighted mean = ΣWX ÷ ΣW — used when items differ in importance.

quiz.q: The main weakness of the arithmetic mean is that it is:
quiz.explanation: Extreme (very large/small) values distort the arithmetic mean.

topics.title: Median
topics.concept:
The median is the middle value of the data when the values are arranged in order (ascending or descending). It divides the data into two equal halves — half the values lie below it and half above. Because it depends on position, not size, the median is not affected by extreme values, which is its great advantage.

To find the median of ungrouped data:

  • First arrange the values in order.
  • If the number of values N is odd, the median is the value at position (N + 1) ÷ 2.
  • If N is even, there are two middle values, and the median is their average.

For example, for 7, 12, 3, 9, 5 — first arrange: 3, 5, 7, 9, 12. N = 5 (odd), so the median is the (5 + 1)÷2 = 3rd value = 7. For 4, 8, 6, 2 — arrange: 2, 4, 6, 8. N = 4 (even), so the median is the average of the 2nd and 3rd values = (4 + 6) ÷ 2 = 5.

The median is a positional average. It is especially useful when the data have extreme values or open-ended classes (like "income above ₹1,00,000"), where the mean cannot be calculated reliably. A related idea: the median is the value of the middle item, and the data can also be split into four quartiles or hundred percentiles in the same positional way.

examples.solution:
Arrange, then take the middle value.

  • Arranged: 8, 11, 15, 19, 22. N = 5 (odd).
  • Median = (5+1)÷2 = 3rd value = 15.

N is even, so average the two middle values.

  • Arranged: 10, 15, 25, 30. N = 4 (even).
  • Median = average of 2nd and 3rd = (15 + 25) ÷ 2 = 20.

examples.problem: Example 3: Why is the median preferred when data have extreme values?
examples.solution:
It depends on position, not size.

  • The median is the middle value, so extreme values do not change it.
examples.answer: Because the median is a positional value (the middle), so extreme values do not affect it.

recap:
• Median = the middle value when data are arranged in order; splits data into two equal halves.
  • Odd N: value at position (N+1)÷2; even N: average of the two middle values.
  • A positional average; not affected by extreme values or open-ended classes.

quiz.q: Unlike the mean, the median is:
quiz.explanation: The median is positional, so extreme values do not affect it.

topics.title: Mode and Comparison of Averages
topics.concept:
The mode is the value that occurs most frequently in the data — the most common or most fashionable value. For example, in 2, 3, 3, 5, 7, 3, 8 the value 3 appears most often, so the mode is 3. Data may have one mode (unimodal), two modes (bimodal) or no mode at all (if every value occurs once). Like the median, the mode is not affected by extreme values, and it can even be found for qualitative data (e.g. the most popular shoe size or the best-selling colour) — which the mean cannot.

So which average should we use? Each has its merits and demerits:

  • Mean — uses all values and is best for further calculation, but is distorted by extreme values and cannot be found for open-ended classes.
  • Median — not affected by extremes and good for open-ended data, but does not use all the values.
  • Mode — simple, works for qualitative data and shows the most typical value, but may not exist or may not be unique.

For a perfectly symmetrical distribution, the three are equal: Mean = Median = Mode. For a moderately skewed distribution they are linked by the empirical relation: Mode = 3 Median − 2 Mean. The practical rule: use the mean for general purposes and further analysis; use the median when there are extreme values or open-ended classes (e.g. average income); and use the mode when you want the most typical/popular item (e.g. the most demanded size of shirt).

examples.solution:
Find the most frequent value.

  • 6 occurs three times, more than any other value.

examples.problem: Example 2: A distribution has Mean = 40 and Median = 38. Estimate the mode.
Example 3: Which average is best for finding the most popular size of shoe sold, and why?
examples.solution:
We want the most frequent item.

  • The mode, because it is the value that occurs most often.
  • It also works for such discrete/qualitative choices.
examples.answer: The mode, because it gives the most frequently occurring (most popular) size.

recap:
• Mode = the most frequently occurring value; not affected by extremes; works for qualitative data; may not exist/be unique.
  • Mean (all values, best for calculation, distorted by extremes); median (positional, good for extremes/open-ended); mode (most typical/popular).
  • Symmetrical: Mean = Median = Mode; skewed: Mode = 3 Median − 2 Mean.

quiz.explanation: 7 occurs most often (three times), so the mode is 7.

quiz.q: For a symmetrical distribution, mean, median and mode are:
quiz.explanation: In a symmetrical distribution, Mean = Median = Mode.

questions.explanation: For odd N, median position = (N+1) ÷ 2.

questions.q: The median is NOT affected by:
questions.explanation: Being positional, the median is unaffected by extreme values.

questions.q: The most frequently occurring value is the:
questions.explanation: The mode is the most frequently occurring value.

questions.explanation: 3 occurs most often (three times).

questions.q: Which average can be found even for qualitative data (e.g. popular colour)?
questions.explanation: The mode works for qualitative data.

questions.q: For a symmetrical distribution, mean, median and mode are:
questions.explanation: They coincide in a symmetrical distribution.

questions.q: The empirical relation among the averages is:
questions.explanation: Mode = 3 Median − 2 Mean (for moderately skewed data).

questions.q: To find the average income where a few people earn very high amounts, the best average is the:
questions.explanation: The median avoids distortion by the few very high incomes.

questions.q: Five workers earn ₹200, ₹250, ₹300, ₹350 and ₹3900. Why does the mean (₹1000) mislead here?
options: One extreme value (₹3900) pulls the mean far above the typical wage
questions.explanation: The single very high wage inflates the mean, so it no longer represents the typical worker — the median (₹300) is better.

questions.q: For the wages in the previous question, the median is:
questions.explanation: Arranged, the middle (3rd of 5) value is ₹300 — unaffected by the extreme ₹3900.

questions.q: A subject with 4 credits scores 70 and a subject with 1 credit scores 95. The weighted mean is:
A shopkeeper wants to stock the most-demanded shirt size. The most useful average is the:
questions.explanation: The mode shows the size that sells most often — exactly what stocking decisions need.

questions.q: A distribution has Mean = 50 and Mode = 44. Using the empirical relation, the median is about:
questions.explanation: Mode = 3 Median − 2 Mean → 44 = 3M − 100 → 3M = 144 → Median = 48.

questions.q: For an income group given as 'above ₹1,00,000' (open-ended), the mean cannot be found, so we use the:
questions.explanation: With an open-ended class there is no mid-value to multiply, so the positional median is used.

questions.q: The mean is preferred for further statistical calculations mainly because it:
options: Uses every value in the data
questions.explanation: Because every observation enters the mean, it is algebraically convenient for further analysis.

questions.q: Data 5, 5, 7, 9, 9 has two modes (5 and 9). Such a distribution is called:
questions.explanation: Two modes make the distribution bimodal.

questions.q: If every value in a data set occurs exactly once, the data have:
questions.explanation: With no repetition, there is no most-frequent value, so there is no mode.

questions.q: Adding ₹100 to every worker's wage raises the mean wage by:
questions.explanation: Adding a constant to every value raises the mean by exactly that constant (₹100).
